category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
Geographic Information Systems (GIS) technology enables the collection, management, analysis, and visualization of location-based data to support informed decision-making. Highlands County utilizes GIS across nearly all departments to improve operational efficiency, enhance public services, and provide residents with accessible geographic information through interactive maps, applications, and other tools.
GIS Day is an annual international celebration recognizing the value of geographic information and the innovative applications of GIS in government, business, and society. It provides an opportunity to acknowledge the contributions of GIS professionals, highlight the technology's impact on our communities, and inspire future generations to explore geospatial technologies.
The proposed proclamation designates November 18, 2026, as GIS Day in Highlands County, recognizing the County's commitment to leveraging GIS technology to better serve its residents.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting

description:
Traditionally, the Board has adopted the same list of holidays observed by the Tenth Judicial Circuit, with minor modifications. Board minutes indicate that in 2012, the Board directed staff to survey the Constitutional Officers concerning the holidays they would be observing. Staff brought back the results of their survey, and from that the Board adopted a schedule of eleven (11) standard holidays they would observe each year and further directed that the list of standard holidays be reflected in the Board’s Personnel Manual. The list has been removed at some point, but the Board’s meeting minutes do not indicate that the Board specifically requested their removal, or increased the number of holidays to be observed each year.
The Tenth Judicial Circuit of Florida has provided their schedule of fourteen holidays for 2027. The following pares down that list; however, there is an additional "Day Before Christmas Eve" holiday the Board voted to observe last year after polling the Constitutional Officers, bringing the total to the twelve (12) holidays staff is recommending as follows:
New Year's Day, Friday, January 1, 2027 (previously approved by the Board on 12/16/25).
Martin Luther King Day, Monday, January 18, 2027
Good Friday, Friday, March 26, 2027
Memorial Day, Monday, May 31, 2027
Independence Day, Monday, July 5, 2027
Labor Day, Monday, September 6, 2027
Veterans Day (Observed), Thursday, November 11, 2027
Thanksgiving Day, Thursday, November 25, 2027
Friday after Thanksgiving, Friday, November 26, 2027
Day Before Christmas Eve, Thursday, December 23, 2027
Christmas Eve, Friday, December 24, 2027
Christmas Day (Observed), Monday, December 27, 2027

description:
Highlands County competitively solicited proposals through RFP 26-014-RDV for strategic planning services for the Highlands County Tourist Development Council (TDC), with London Tourism Publications, Inc. selected to provide these services. The proposed agreement provides for the development of a comprehensive tourism strategic plan with measurable goals and a roadmap to strengthen the TDC and guide future tourism growth in Highlands County. The scope includes evaluation of the TDC’s organizational structure and governance, stakeholder and visitor research, tourism asset and gap analysis, seasonal visitation analysis, and estimates of annual visitation and room nights.
The total agreement is $53,000, inclusive of all professional services, research, facilitation, report preparation, presentations, project management and travel expenses. Highlands County has been awarded a $50,000 Community Planning Technical Assistance (CPTA) grant from the State of Florida to assist with the cost of developing the Strategic Plan, with the remaining $3,000 funded through Fund 152 (Tourist Development Trust). The completed Strategic Plan is due April 15, 2027, and will be presented to the TDC at its April 2027 quarterly meeting.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
The Capital Improvements Element (CIE) of the Highlands County 2050 Comprehensive Plan considers the County’s need for and location of public facilities and infrastructure. The CIE establishes policies to ensure that adequate public facilities are available to meet established acceptable levels of service (LOS) for existing and future development, consistent with the requirements of Section 163.3177(3)(a), Florida Statutes. This includes consideration of the impacts of new development on facilities such as roads, parks and recreation, drainage, water and wastewater systems, and schools.
The CIE is required to include a schedule of capital improvement projects necessary to achieve and maintain adopted LOS standards for at least a five-year period, along with the funding sources for those projects. Section 163.3177(3)(a), Florida Statutes, requires the Capital Improvement Schedule (CIS) within the CIE to be updated annually to reflect the County’s current capital improvement priorities and available funding. These proposed changes to the CIS correspond to the ten-year Capital Financial Strategy (CFS) adopted by the Highlands County Board of County Commissioners on September 15, 2026 as part of the Fiscal Year 2026/2027 annual budget. While the CFS identifies planned capital spending over the next ten years, the CIS specifically identifies projects related to public facilities for which LOS standards are identified within the CIE.
The Planning and Zoning Commission recommended approval of CIS 2026-2027 at their October 13, 2026 meeting by a vote of 7-0.
This public hearing has been duly noticed and published, and proof of publication has been provided to the Clerk to be made part of the permanent record.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
On November 5, 1992, the County adopted Ordinance No. 92-22, creating the Historic Preservation Commission (HPC) and establishing a framework for the designation and protection of historic properties and districts, including review of activities that could affect designated resources. The first seven HPC members were appointed on June 22, 1993. No properties or districts were designated under the original ordinance.
In 1999, Highlands County was designated as a Florida Certified Local Government (CLG) by the Florida Department of State, Division of Historical Resources. CLG participation established ongoing program responsibilities, including maintaining an active preservation commission that meets at least four times annually, identifying and documenting historic resources, participating in National Register of Historic Places nomination reviews, and providing opportunities for public participation. The County's local preservation ordinance separately authorizes the HPC to review activities affecting locally designated historic properties. In 2007, the County designated ten properties as local historic properties through Ordinance No. 06-07-38.County staff has reviewed the HPC's CLG-related and ordinance-authorized activities since 2007 and determined the following:One designated property was demolished in 2010, for which staff has not located a record of HPC review or approval, and the property was annexed into the City of Avon Park in 2016.
In 2023, the owners of another designated property requested removal of the property from the County's local historic designation list.
Staff identified only one review of an activity involving a locally designated property during this period: a 2026 review of a new caretaker's residence at the Pearce-Lockett Estate. That review also identified previous alterations and demolitions for which no HPC review or approval was located.
Four historic survey projects were completed, resulting in no additional local designations.
The HPC participated in four National Register nomination reviews and two reviews of potential ad valorem historic property tax exemption projects.
A review of historical HPC agendas also shows that much of the Commission's work over its approximately 30-year history has focused on education, outreach, and promotion. Activities have included newspaper articles, brochures, websites, displays, historic plaques, proclamations, and coordination with local historical societies. These efforts have helped increase public awareness of the County's history and historic resources, but they have not led to further designations or protection of any of the properties which are currently designated as historic.
The limited number of reviews involving locally designated properties, the absence of additional local designations resulting from survey efforts, and the limited number of other preservation-related reviews indicate that the existing commission-centered regulatory structure has seen limited use. This is not a reflection on the commitment or contributions of individual Commission members. Rather, it raises the question of whether the existing structure remains appropriate for the historic preservation needs and level of activity in Highlands County.
While the County can continue to recognize, document, and promote its historic and cultural resources, these objectives do not necessarily require a standing regulatory commission or continued participation in a program with ongoing administrative requirements. Education and outreach can continue through partnerships with local historical societies, museums, tourism organizations, and other community groups.
The ongoing required updates to the Highlands County Comprehensive Plan will also provide an opportunity to evaluate how historic, cultural, and archaeological resources should be identified and considered in the County's planning and development review processes. Any future preservation efforts can be structured around the County's actual needs, with staff coordination and appropriately tailored regulatory protections where warranted.

Part 800, the regulations governing Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) of 1966. Section 106 requires federal agencies to consider the effects of projects they carry out, fund, permit, license, or approve on historic properties. The proposed revisions would change the opportunities for local governments, Tribes, other consulting parties, and the public to provide information and participate in Section 106 review before federal decisions are made.

description:
At the request of the Board of County Commissioners, the County Attorney’s Office initiated the process of updating the various Committees, Boards, and Commissions (collectively referred to as “Committee(s)”) established by the Highlands County Board of County Commissioners. These updates aim to streamline the process for member appointments to all Committees created by Highlands County. On October 15, 2024, the Board approved Ordinance 24-25-02, establishing a consistent and more refined process for the appointment, removal, membership, and terms of members of the various Committees established by the County that are not governed by Florida law.
Following the adoption of Ordinance 24-25-02, the County Attorney’s Office team began the process of updating each Committee’s governing document to reflect the principles adopted by the Board.
The Natural Resources Advisory Commission (NRAC) was established by Highlands County on February 5, 1991, to provide a forum for the consideration of natural resource issues affecting the County. On August 18, 2015, the Board adopted Resolution No. 14-15-89, establishing protocols for NRAC’s composition, nominations, appointments, rotation, elections, meetings, mission, and authority. The Board subsequently adopted Resolution No. 20-21-98 in June 2021, amending the composition and meeting schedule of NRAC. The proposed Resolution updates NRAC consistent with the guidelines established by Ordinance 24-25-02.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Request approval of Resolution No.: 26-27-35 updating the structure of the Natural Resources Advisory Committee.

Since 2007, the Ounce of Prevention Fund of Florida, administrator of the Healthy Families Florida program, has sub-contracted with Highlands County as the local lead entity to provide home-visiting services to eligible county residents. The contract was renewed for FY 2026–2027 on June 16, 2026, however, subsequent to the renewal, select sites within the Healthy Families Florida network were notified of funding reductions for FY 2026–2027. Healthy Families Highlands’ funding reduction totals $84,458, resulting in a revised grant award of $259,005 to provide services through June 30, 2027.
An amendment to the existing contract is necessary to reflect the revised grant award and corresponding cash contribution match, which was included in the County’s adopted FY 2026–2027 budget. Approval of this amendment will allow for the continued delivery of home-visiting services to eligible Highlands County families through June 30, 2027.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
The Affordable Housing Advisory Committee was created by Ordinance to review the established policies, procedures, ordinances, land development regulations and adopt a comprehensive plan of the County, and to recommend specific initiatives to encourage or facilitate affordable housing while protecting the ability of the property to appreciate in value.
The Committee consists of at least 8, but not more than 11 members, and includes at least one local elected county official. Members must be representatives from the following categories:
(Seat 1) One citizen who is actively engaged in the banking or mortgage industry in connection with affordable housing.
(Seat 2) One citizen who is actively engaged as an advocate for low-income persons in connection with affordable housing.
(Seat 3) One citizen who is actively engaged in the residential home building industry in connection with affordable housing. (VACANT)
(Seat 4) One citizen who is actively engaged as a real estate professional in connection with affordable housing. (VACANT)
(Seat 5) One citizen who is a representative of those areas of labor actively engaged in home building in connection with affordable housing.
(Seat 6) One citizen who represents employers within the jurisdiction of Highlands County.
(Seat 7) One citizen who resides within the jurisdiction of Highlands County.
(Seat 8) One citizen who actively serves on the local planning agency pursuant to F.S. § 163.3174.
(Seat 9) One citizen who represents essential services personnel, as defined in the Highlands County Housing Assistance Program. (VACANT)
(Seat 10) One citizen who is actively engaged as a for-profit provider of affordable housing. (VACANT)
(Seat 11) One citizen who is actively engaged as a not-for-profit provider of affordable housing.
This vacancy occurred 6/17/26 when staff received notification from Audrey Ascuitto, who held Seat # 4, (One citizen who is actively engaged as a real estate professional in connection with affordable housing) that she would be resigning from her seat. Beginning mid-June 2026, notice of this vacancy was publicly advertised through multiple channels, including the County website, targeted emails and outreach to lenders, Heartland Association of Realtors, closing agencies and social media platforms. The vacancy is still actively being advertised. Staff received 2 (two) applications and the applications were reviewed and confirmed by staff to meet the eligibility criteria established by Ordinance 21-22-08.
According to Ordinance 21-22-08, members shall serve for two-year terms, and may be reappointed for subsequent terms.
Attached for your review and consideration are the applications submitted by Mr. Eric Rhoades and Mrs. Elsa Jane Miller and the Ordinance.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Request to appoint one (1) member to the Affordable Housing Advisory Committee to fill vacant Seat #4 (one citizen who is actively engaged as a real estate professional in connection with affordable housing)

Commissioner Arlene Tuck

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
Geographic Information Systems (GIS) technology has rapidly become a strategic and core business enabler for local government while serving as an invaluable analytical and communications tool deployed by the County. Mapping products are becoming increasingly more integrated in the provision of public services. Environmental Systems Research Institute, Inc. (ESRI) is the vendor of the GIS software that the County has been using for many years. Over time, the County’s adoption of the ESRI suite of products has grown substantially.
Historically, Highlands County has had an agreement with Environmental Systems Research Institute, Inc. (ESRI) for a Small Municipal and County Government Enterprise License Agreement (ELA). The ELA is a three-year agreement that grants the County access to ESRI license software including support on all software offered through the ELA for the term of the agreement. County staff is requesting renewal and approval of the ELA Agreement with ESRI.
Under the proposed agreement, the County will acquire ESRI software products, maintenance and support services that are unique and proprietary to the vendor and not available from an alternate source.
The total cost of the three-year agreement is $270,900.00 to be paid in three equal annual payments of $90,300.00. This is an increase of $95,400 over 3 (three) years or an additional $31,800 per year. The agreement provided from ESRI includes technical support and four complimentary annual conference registrations at no additional cost.
RECOMMENDED ACTION
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
Florida Statutes, Chapter 406, requires that the County arrange for the final disposition of human remains at the expense of the public when the remains are unclaimed or when a decedent qualifies as indigent. Highlands County recognizes its responsibility to provide for the dignified disposition of eligible indigent and unclaimed human remains when no other person or entity has both the legal responsibility and financial ability to do so.
Highlands County has established a "Cremation Only" practice which means that disposition of human remains at the expense of the County shall be only through the use of cremation, except when prohibited by law or regulations and/or the identity of the decedent is unknown. This allows the body to be exhumed, if necessary for future identification.
Highlands County will only authorize payments to contracted funeral homes, not exceeding the established contractual rate.

attachments.name: Letter of Support Man Up and Go

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description: Man Up and Go does more than tell men to "do better." Its trained coaches walk alongside fathers, helping them set practical goals around employment, stability, sobriety, healthy relationships, parenting, and accountability. For fathers involved with child welfare, this support can be critical to navigating reunification, meeting requirements, rebuilding trust, and becoming active in their children's lives. Under the leadership of CEO Jeff Ford, Man Up and Go has built a culture of excellence, relationships, grit, and long-term commitment. The organization serves fathers seeking reunification, mentors boys and young men affected by foster care, promotes healthy masculinity, and supports foster, adoptive, kinship, and reunified families. Man Up and Go has supported 199 caregivers and 451 children, mobilized more than 1,200 volunteer hours, and delivered over 6,000 practical support services to families, including meals, counseling assistance, respite, household support, and individualized assistance.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Letter of Support Man Up and Go Inc.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
The Period of PURPLE Crying Program is an evidence-based shaken baby syndrome/abusive head trauma prevention program designed to help caregivers understand and respond appropriately to increased infant crying. The program provides caregivers with strategies to manage the challenges associated with persistent crying and helps prevent abusive head trauma that can result when a baby is shaken in frustration.
The Period of PURPLE Crying Program was first implemented as part of Healthy Families Highlands services in October 2025. Renewal of the service agreement between the Ounce of Prevention Fund of Florida and Highlands County will allow Healthy Families Highlands to continue providing the Period of PURPLE Crying curriculum and related services to program participants.
Under the renewed agreement, Healthy Families Highlands will receive a one-time payment of $2,500 to support the implementation of the program and delivery of its services to participating families.

description: The Florida Housing Finance Corporation (FHFC) administers the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP), which allocates funds to local governments as an incentive to create partnerships that produce and preserve affordable homeownership. SHIP funds are distributed on an entitlement basis to all 67 counties and 57 Community Development Block Grant entitlement cities in Florida. Submitting an annual report detailing the process of the SHIP Program to the FHFC is an essential element of program administration. To receive future funding, all jurisdictions are required to report annually on local affordable housing program expenditures and demographic data. Once the report has been submitted and accepted as true and accurate, a certification form must be signed by the Chief Elected Official and submitted to FHFC.

attachments.name: Resolution 25-26-161 Vulnerability Assessment with Final Report Exhibits

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
Highlands County was awarded a Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) Grant (Agreement #23PLN113) to conduct a comprehensive countywide Vulnerability Assessment pursuant to Section 380.093, Florida Statutes. The Vulnerability Assessment included coordination with and analysis of the municipalities of Avon Park, Lake Placid, and Sebring. The County worked with the Central Florida Regional Planning Council (CFRPC) to complete the Grant Work Plan.
The final Vulnerability Assessment includes:
Results and conclusions, including illustrations via maps and tables, based on the statutorily required scenarios and standards in s. 380.093, F.S.
A list of critical and regionally significant assets within the county that are impacted by flooding. The list of critical and regionally significant assets is prioritized by area or immediate need and identifies which flood scenario(s) impacts each asset.
Electronic mapping data used to illustrate flooding and sea level rise impacts identified in the Vulnerability Assessment, to include the geospatial data in an electronic file format and GIS metadata.
With additional funding from the Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership (CHNEP), three priority Adaptation Action Area plans were developed, providing detailed recommendations for improvements that could be made to mitigate the impacts of flooding on critical and regionally significant assets. These plans are included as an appendix to the completed Vulnerability Assessment.

25-26-096 Add'l Fds_Replace Discharge Line, Scale Repairs (BA)

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
BA 25-26-096 is requesting additional funding for the replacement of the pump discharge line and repair of the scale system. Prior to disassembly, the exterior of the existing discharge line, which is more than 30 years old, appeared to be in satisfactory condition. However, once the system was dismantled, the contractor discovered significant deterioration in the interior of the pipe. Based on this condition, the contractor strongly recommends replacing the discharge line. Failure to do so could result in improper pump operation and may potentially damage the new pump. The estimated cost to replace the discharge line, including materials, parts, and labor, is approximately $32,000. Additionally, the scale system appears to have sustained damage from a lightning strike and is currently inoperable. The estimated cost to repair the scale system is approximately $12,000.
Also, operating account budgets are in the negative and need additional funding, so this budget amendment is providing adequate funds for the balance of the year.
The total additional funding requested is $79,000.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
Attached for your review and approval is the FDEP Highlands County Master Stormwater Plan & Thunderbird Road Drainage Improvements Grant #LO213 and resolution 25-26-137 authorizing the Chairman of the Board to execute said Agreement for Highlands County Project Number 25050. Due to existing collapsed drainage pipes the conveyance of stormwater within Highlands County has been reduced, causing structural flooding. Highlands County intends to create a master stormwater plan to identify needs for construction of water quality and quantity features to better control stormwater conveyance and reduce total maximum daily loads (TMDL), mainly nitrogen and phosphorous, from entering the watershed. The project will reduce ongoing maintenance costs, provide risk reduction from flooding, and provide a vision for future drainage projects.
The Board Attorney has reviewed and approved the FDEP Highlands County Master Stormwater Plan & Thunderbird Road Drainage Improvements and accompanying resolution. Donald Carey, PE, Assistant County Engineer – Stormwater is the project manager for this project under the direct supervision of the County Engineer.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting

description: Following the success of the 2025 Last Paddler Standing event, organizers have confirmed their desire to return to H.L. Bishop Park for the 2026 event scheduled for December 5–7, 2026. Similar to 2025, a special License Agreement is required to authorize overnight use of the facility for this multi-day sports tourism event. The proposed agreement would permit temporary use of designated park areas for overnight access, extended operating hours, participant rest areas, event staging, vendor setup, parking, safety monitoring, and related logistical operations. Last Paddler Standing attracts competitors, support crews, and spectators from across the globe, generating visitor spending and overnight stays in Highlands County. In addition to the onsite event impact, organizers have offered the Highlands County Tourist Development Council advertising opportunities during the event’s 48+ hour live stream, social media promotion, and related media content, providing added destination exposure. The live broadcast is also archived online, creating ongoing visibility for Highlands County as an outdoor recreation and sports tourism destination. Approval of the agreement would allow Highlands County to host the returning event while maximizing both economic impact and promotional value.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
The Affordable Housing Advisory Committee was created by Ordinance to review the established policies, procedures, ordinance, land development regulations and adopted comprehensive plan of the County, and to recommend specific initiatives to encourage or facilitate affordable housing while protecting the ability of the property to appreciate in value.
The Committee consists of at least 8, but not more than 11 members, and includes at least one local elected county official. Members must be representatives from the following categories:
(1) One citizen who is actively engaged in the banking or mortgage industry in connection with affordable housing. (VACANT)
(2) One citizen who is actively engaged as an advocate for low-income persons in connection with affordable housing.
(3) One citizen who is actively engaged in the residential home building industry in connection with affordable housing. (VACANT)
(4) One citizen who is actively engaged as a real estate professional in connection with affordable housing. (VACANT)
(5) One citizen who is a representative of those areas of labor actively engaged in home building in connection with affordable housing.
(6) One citizen who represents employers within the jurisdiction of Highlands County.
(7) One citizen who resides within the jurisdiction of Highlands County.
(8) One citizen who actively serves on the local planning agency pursuant to F.S. § 163.3174.
(9) One citizen who represents essential services personnel, as defined in the Highlands County Housing Assistance Program. (VACANT)
(10) One citizen who is actively engaged as a for-profit provider of affordable housing. (VACANT)
(11) One citizen who is actively engaged as a not-for-profit provider of affordable housing.
This vacancy occurred December 2023 when staff received notification from Doritza Lobozzo, who held Seat #1, (one citizen who is actively engaged in the banking or mortgage industry in connection with affordable housing) that she would be resigning from her seat. Beginning January 2024, notice of this vacancy was publicly advertised through multiple channels, including the County website, targeted email outreach to lenders, closing agencies and social media platforms. The vacancy is still actively being advertised. Staff received only 1 application and the application was reviewed and confirmed by staff to meet the eligibility criteria established by Ordinance 21-22-08.
According to Ordinance 21-22-08, members shall serve for two-year terms, and may be reappointed for subsequent terms.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Appointment of Elsie Sellers to the Affordable Housing Advisory Committee. ($0)

description: Pursuant to Florida Statute 125.0104, two members of the Tourist Development Council (TDC) must be elected municipal officials, with at least one representative from the municipality with the largest population in the county. In Highlands County, the second municipal elected official seat has historically alternated between the Town of Lake Placid and the City of Avon Park in four-year terms. The term most recently held by a representative from the Town of Lake Placid expired on June 30, 2026. Consistent with past practice, staff contacted the City of Avon Park to request a recommendation for appointment to the upcoming term. On May 28, 2026, City Manager Jason Atkinson confirmed that the City recommends Council Member Brittany McGuire for appointment to the TDC.

category: Special Meeting of the Board of County Commissioners
description:
This ordinance adopts the 2026 Impact Fee Study and establishes updated fee rates, which will be phased in over several years until full rates are reached. It defines how fees are calculated, when they are due, and how they are applied to different types of development.
It establishes benefit districts that determine where fees are collected and how they may be spent. It also sets rules for refunds if permits are cancelled or if fees are not used within the required timeframes.
The ordinance allows developers to request alternative fee calculations based on project-specific data, and it provides credits when developers build or dedicate improvements that reduce public infrastructure needs.
It requires updates to the fee study and ongoing reporting, auditing, and certification of how funds are collected and spent. It also establishes an appeals process for disputes.

description: Ordinance 25-26-16 amends Section 8-221 of the Highlands County Code of Ordinances relating to the collection and administration of the Tourist Development Tax. The ordinance provides for the transfer of Tourist Development Tax collection, administration, enforcement, and audit responsibilities from the Florida Department of Revenue (FDOR) to the Highlands County Tax Collector, as authorized by Section 125.0104, Florida Statutes. The Highlands County Tourist Development Council recommended the transfer on October 30, 2025, and the Highlands County Tax Collector has agreed to assume these responsibilities. By collecting locally, this change is expected to improve customer service, increase local oversight, and allow a more streamlined remittance of revenues. The proposed changes would become effective for the October 2026 collection period, with returns due beginning November 1, 2026.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
Highlands County Fire Rescue (Highlands County) is seeking approval to apply for an Assistance to Firefighters Grant (AFG) in the amount of $2,000,000. A critical and immediate need exists to replace aging aerial apparatus that have exceeded their useful service life and are no longer capable of reliably supporting emergency response operations.
HCFR currently operates two aging aerial apparatus: Ladder 36, a 1994 Pierce Saber 100-foot aerial platform, and Quint 29, a 1997 E-One 50-foot Quint. Ladder 36 was recently placed out of service after failing a critical hydraulic stabilization component during its 2025 aerial certification inspection. Both the manufacturer and third-party vendors have confirmed that replacement parts are no longer available, making recertification and continued operation impossible. The apparatus has accumulated approximately 102,456 miles and has exceeded its expected service life.
To address this urgent operational need, HCFR has identified an in-production demonstration aerial apparatus available for approximately $2.2 million. Purchasing this apparatus would provide an immediate cost savings of approximately $220,000 compared to a newly ordered equivalent unit, which is estimated to cost $2.42 million. Acquisition of the demonstration unit would allow HCFR to restore aerial response capabilities more quickly while maximizing the value of grant funding.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Request approval to apply for the Assistance to Firefighters Grant (AFG) Application.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
As part of the Ridge to River Conservation Planning Study, the Board approved moving forward to polling at the February 3, 2026, meeting. Polling consisted of a series of questions to Highlands County registered voters. The results of those polls are presented as follows.
Based on the polling results and the recommendation of the Trust for Public Land, we are asking the Board to decide whether to move forward with a ballot referendum for November 2026.
If moving forward, the title and summary of the referendum to appear on the ballot shall read as follows:
Bonds establishing land conservation program to protect and improve: water resources, agricultural lands, wildlife corridors.
Shall Highlands County fund an environmentally sensitive lands program, preserving lands from development by acquiring property interests to improve and protect water resources, agricultural lands and wildlife corridors, for conservation and resource-based recreation, by issuing bonds up to $20 million, maturing within 20 years, bearing interest not exceeding the maximum legal rate, payable from ad valorem tax not exceeding 0.25 mill, subject to full public disclosure of all spending?
Moving forward, it will allow the residents of Highlands County to vote if a conservation program is wanted to purchase qualifying lands and conservation easements to protect our water resources like drinking water, working agricultural lands, and preservation of the wildlife corridor throughout Highlands County.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Update on Ridge to River Conservation Program polling results and direction on referendum approval.

attachments.name: CAC Victim Services Specialist  AMENDED FINAL 12.22.23

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
The Children’s Advocacy Center (CAC) is requesting approval to modify its current staffing structure to better align with mental health program operations and service needs. The request is to eliminate one part-time Mental Health therapist position and the part-time Victim Support Specialist position and create one full-time Mental Health therapist position.
The CAC operates within a multidisciplinary team (MDT) model, providing coordinated services to child victims of abuse and their families. Mental health services are an essential component of this model and are required to ensure continuity of care and compliance with program standards.
Recent updates to State Attorney’s Office (SAO) guidelines have expanded the scope of forensic interviews to include all presenting abuse types and allegations, rather than limiting interviews to sexual abuse cases. As a result, an increase in referrals to the CAC is anticipated.
Both current part-time Mental Health Therapists are operating at capacity, with a caseload of approximately 15 clients each, which is the maximum manageable level for that position. Additionally, the CAC has started a waiting list for therapy clients due to recent high demand. The existing staffing structure does not adequately support the anticipated increase in service demand or ensure consistency in service delivery. Adjustments are needed to improve scheduling, case management, and overall service coordination.
Both part-time Mental Health Therapist positions are currently 100% grant funded. The CAC will continue to utilize every grant option available to cover the expenses of the new FTE position and the continued PT position. The fiscal impact of a move from part-time to full-time would be an increase of $26,246.00 annually. However, the elimination of the part-time Victim Support Specialist position causes a reduction of approximately $23,410.00. Therefore, the net increase would be approximately $2,836.00.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Request to approve eliminating two part-time CAC positions and creating one full-time Therapist position ($2,836.00).

description:
Following direction from the Board of County Commissioners during its review of the Statement of Legislative Intent, staff has prepared proposed revisions to Article 4, Plats, Site Plans, and Improvement Plans. These changes align with SB 784, which streamlines the plat approval process by establishing review timelines and transferring approval authority from elected officials to administrative staff.
It has been determined that certain provisions in the Highlands County Land Development Regulations (LDRs), specifically those governing the application process for plat recording within Article 4, Plats, Site Plans, and Improvement Plans, require updates to ensure consistency with SB 784. To comply with the statute, the LDRs must be amended by ordinance to delegate plat and replat recording authority to the appropriate administrative official or department and to establish written procedures and timelines that meet the statutory notice and review requirements.
These actions will ensure local compliance with the updated statute and align internal processes with the Legislature’s intent to create uniform timelines for the plat recording review.
These revisions were presented before the Planning & Zoning Commission on April 14, 2026, as P&Z 2188 and were approved unanimously.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Public Hearing to consider proposed amendments to the Highlands County Code of Ordinances, Chapter 12, Land Development Regulations, Article 4, Plats, Site Plans and Improvement Plans and Division 1, Development Orders, Section 12.04.112, Final Plat.

Everyone who has worked with Nancy knows that no matter the time of day or night, she was there when we needed her.
From multiple hurricane activations to community events, Nancy was always actively involved and fully engaged. She made it a priority to ensure that our needs and concerns were addressed quickly, professionally, and effectively. Her dedication and responsiveness played a key role in strengthening the partnership we value today with Duke Energy.
Nancy’s professionalism, reliability, and commitment to service never went unnoticed. She has been a trusted partner and a true advocate for our community, and her impact will be felt long after her retirement.
We thank Nancy for her years of service, her unwavering support of Highlands County, and the relationships she helped build. She will be greatly missed, and we congratulate her on 34 remarkable years and wish her all the best in her well-earned retirement.

attachments.name: Highlands County Historic Preservation Month Proclamation

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description: Since the National Trust for Historic Preservation ("the Trust") created Historic Preservation Week in 1971 to spotlight grassroots preservation efforts in America, it has grown into an annual celebration observed by small towns and big cities throughout the country. Due to its overwhelming popularity, in 2005 the Trust extended the celebration to the entire month of May by declaring it Preservation Month, to provide an even longer opportunity to celebrate the diverse and unique heritage of our country’s cities and states and to enable more Americans to become involved in the growing preservation movement. Highlands County, as a Certified Local Government with the Division of Historical Resources within the Florida Department of State, is part of a statewide preservation partnership to revitalize neighborhoods and communities, spark economic development and promote environmental sustainability. In conjunction with the State’s celebration of May as Historic Preservation Month, and the commemoration of our nation's 250th anniversary this year, members of our Highlands County Historic Preservation Commission ask the Board to approve a Proclamation designating May 2026, as Highlands County Historic Preservation Month.

title: Request approval of a Proclamation recognizing May 2026, as "Historic Preservation Month" in Highlands County

Amendment No. 2 to the Ajax Building Company construction agreement reflects a revised scope of work necessary to support operational requirements for the jail expansion project. The additional work includes the installation of two generators and the construction of a secure corridor connecting the existing jail to the new expansion — elements that were not part of the original plan set dated August 30, 2024.
The generator study and associated drawings were finalized on August 28, 2025. The increased electrical load and operational needs identified in that study require expanded electrical and mechanical infrastructure to ensure the new building integrates properly with the existing jail systems. These upgrades are essential for maintaining reliable power, life-safety systems, and continuity of operations.
Secure corridor drawings were completed on November 12, 2025. This connection is critical for coordinating work within an occupied jail facility and for establishing proper sequencing, controlled access, and operational constraints from the sally port into the jail. The corridor ensures staff and inmate movement can be maintained without disrupting daily jail operations.
The expanded scope of work has increased both the complexity and duration of the project. These additions are necessary to support long-term operational functionality, safety, and compliance within the integrated jail campus.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
At their October 30, 2025 Meeting, the Tourist Development Council (TDC) voted unanimously to recommend allocating all Asset Development/Enhancement funds collected through the Tourist Development Tax (TDT) towards the expansion of the Highlands County Mulit-Sport Complex and the future development of an indoor multi-purpose facility.
When the Highlands County Tourist Development Tax (TDT) increased to 4% in 2018, one percent, often referred to as the "3rd-penny", was designated by the Tourist Development Council (TDC) to be set aside from TDT collections for the development and enhancement of facilities that attract tournaments, events, and visitors who generate overnight stays in Highlands County. These funds have been accumulated since 2018 and are held within Fund 152 (Tourist Development Trust) in the Asset Development/Enhancement fund balance.
Based on project funding estimates presented to the TDC on October 30, 2025, and to the Board of County Commissioners during the Facility Development Workshop on November 4, 2025, the TDC recommends appropriating $1,900,000.00 of the "3rd penny" collections to complete the expansion of the Highlands County Multi-Sport Complex, representing the full estimated funding needed for that project. The remaining balance of the “3rd penny” collections is recommended to be allocated toward the development of a future indoor multi-purpose facility. The TDC intends to continue designating future annual collections from this funding source toward the indoor facility in order to reach the estimated total project cost of approximately $4,250,000.
These investments are intended to strengthen Highlands County’s ability to attract sporting events and visitors, supporting overnight stays and generating positive economic impact for the community.

A new opioid settlement proposal has been sent to the County arising out of nationwide opioid litigation. This new proposal represents a settlement with numerous local governments throughout the United States. This settlement does not include the Florida Attorney General nor any allocation for the State of Florida nor any other state.
The current proposed settlement includes six regional distributors and dispensers of opioid products. Those entities are: Associated Pharmacies, Inc. (and American Associated Pharmacies), J M Smith Corporation, Louisiana Wholesale Drug Company, Inc., Morris and Dickson Co., North Carolina Mutual Wholesale Drug Company, Inc. and United Natural Foods, Inc. (including its subsidiaries SuperValu and Advantage Logistics) (collectively the "Six Remnant Defendants").
This proposed settlement is an opt-in settlement. Whether or not the settlement moves forward depends upon the level of participation. If the settlement moves forward, the defendants agree to pay a combined total of $97,625,000.00 for purposes of abating the opioid epidemic. Highlands County would receive a portion of those settlement funds in a one-time payment.
Eligible entities, such as counties, municipalities, and other local subdivisions, may participate by opting in by Monday, May 4, 2026.

description: Chapter 9, Article V, Highlands County Code of Ordinances currently provides for a landowner-based election process for the governing Board of the Sun ’n Lake of Sebring Improvement District.Since the Sun ’n Lake of Sebring Improvement District (“District”) was originally established in 1974, by Highlands County Ordinance No.: 74-4. The District was created prior to the enactment of modern Florida independent special district law (Chapter 189, Florida Statutes) which requires a special act of the Legislature; however, the structure of the District does not fully align with the dependent special district criteria either. The proposed agreement term is for up to three (3) years or until completion of the identified projects, in an amount not to exceed $475,000 total, or $237,500 per project.
Synergy Sports previously completed the County’s sports facility feasibility study and has been involved in prior phases of this effort. Based on this prior work, Synergy has familiarity with the County’s objectives, site considerations, and stakeholder input, and has been determined to be uniquely qualified to provide continued consulting services.
Past TDC meetings where relevant presentations and prior actions took place include:Apr. 25, 2024: Indoor Facility Business Plan presented by Synergy Sports
Oct. 31, 2024: Approved moving forward with separate indoor/outdoor concepts and appraisal for expansion land for Sports Complex
Dec. 16, 2024 (Special Meeting): Directed staff to negotiate purchase of expansion property and proceed to BOCC
Jan. 29, 2026: Approved continued services with Synergy Sports for next phase of work (subsequently consolidated into current agreement)
Past BCC Meetings where relevant presentations and prior actions took place include:Nov. 4, 2025 (Workshop): Workshop discussion on sports complex expansion and indoor facility development.
Dec. 2, 2025: Approved Real Property Purchase Agreement for land to expand the complex.
Mar. 3, 2026: Approved DEP reimbursable grant for 50% of land acquisition.
Approval of this agreement will allow the County to continue coordinated planning and development of both the outdoor complex expansion and the proposed indoor facility.

description:
Attached for your review and approval is the Small County Outreach Program (SCOP) Agreement between Florida Departmant of Transportation (FDOT) and Highlands County, and Resolution 25-26-096 authorizing the Chairman of the Board to execute said Agreement for Highlands County Project Number 25039 for the design, construction, and construction engineering inspection (CEI) for the widening and resurfacing of CR 731 from Clubhouse Road to the Baptist Church. Also included for your review and approval is Resolution 25-26-25-26-113 for Budget Amendment 25-26-25-26-077 to appropriate the funds for this project.
FDOT is willing to provide the County with financial assistance under the FDOT Financial Project No. 450323-1-54-01. The proposed construction consists of widening and resurfacing of CR 731 from Clubhouse Road to the Baptist Church. The County shall be responsible for ensuring that the construction work under this agreement is performed in accordance with the approved construction documents and that it will meet all applicable FDOT standards. It is the County’s intent for the design, and construction to be done by in-house forces and for the CEI to be contracted out.
In the event the County proceeds with any phase of the Project utilizing its own forces, the County will only be reimbursed for direct costs (this excludes general overhead).
The County shall commence the project activities after the execution of this Agreement and shall perform in accordance with the following schedule:
1. Design to be completed on or before December 31, 2028.
2. Right-of-Way to be certified on or before December 31, 2028.
3. Construction contract to be let on or before June 30, 2029.
4. Construction to be completed on or before June 30, 2031.
The Board Attorney has reviewed and approved the FDOT SCOP Agreement and the accompanying resolution. Kenya Anderson is the project manager for this project under the direct supervision of the Assistant County Engineer. The Assistant County Engineer will be the engineer of record.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
The Community Programs Division currently operates with a Community Programs Specialist position classified at a pay grade 104. Over time, the scope and complexity of this role has expanded significantly due to increased program demand, heightened reporting requirements, needed interdepartmental coordination, case management/referral services, and the need for stronger fiscal and performance oversight. The current classification no longer accurately reflects the level of responsibility or accountability required to effectively perform in the capacity needed.
The current job title and classification limits the County's ability to effectively administer community programs, ensure compliance, and maintain high service standards. The role has evolved beyond technical and program support functions into one requiring coordination, oversight, and independent resource and referral decision-making. Without reclassification of this position, there is a risk of reduced operational efficiency, staff turnover due to misaligned compensation, and potential gaps in program accountability.
Reclassifying the Community Programs Specialist position to a Community Programs Coordinator (pay grade 107) formally recognizes and incorporates the following responsibilities:
- Providing information, assistance and referrals.
- Supporting community engagement efforts including workshops, public meetings, and outreach events.
- Maintaining program records.
- Providing case management.
- Performing administrative duties in support of the Community Programs department.
- Collaborating with nonprofit organizations, community groups, and other county departments to support program goals.
Reclassifying the position of Community Programs Coordinator to Community Programs Specialist is a fiscally responsible adjustment that reflects current operational needs of the County. This change will ensure that programs are managed effectively, resources are used efficiently, and the County continues to deliver high-quality services to the community while maintaining prudent financial stewardship.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Request approval of reclassification of Community Programs Specialist to Community Programs Coordinator.($5,750)

description: The Highlands County Board of County Commissioners applied for and was awarded a Resiliency Planning Grant through the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. This grant (titled Highlands County Comprehensive Vulnerability Assessment Including Avon Park, Sebring and Lake Placid) assesses the vulnerability of the critical assets against extreme rainfall and flooding. This project will be used to help build the community’s resilience by predicting potential depth of water from flooding, analyzing potential impacts on critical assets, potential impacts on different demographic groups, and will serve as the basis for building resilience. Using the information gathered from the vulnerability assessment, the County and cities will be able to identify potential improvements to the critical assets impacted by potential floodwaters. Completing the vulnerability assessment, in accordance with the criteria outlined in Florida Statutes, qualifies the County and the cities for additional FDEP project funding through Resilient Florida or other FDEP grants. Staff from the Central Florida Regional Planning Council will provide a project update.

The proposed amendments to the Plan are based on a review of changes in Florida Statutes since the last time the Plan was updated and a review of the Comprehensive Plan against existing conditions, requirements of the Land Development Regulations, and input from the community. The Plan's current planning period extends to the year 2030. The long-term planning period of the Plan will be updated to the year 2050, consistent with Section 163.3177, Florida Statutes. category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
Sunshine Sunday was established in Florida in 2002, initiated by the Florida Society of Newspaper Editors. In 2005, National Sunshine Week was launched by the American Society of Newspaper Editors with support from the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation.Sunshine Week takes place annually in mid-March, aligning with the birthday of James Madison on March 16 (1751). Madison was instrumental in the 1787 Constitutional Convention and presented the first version of the Bill of Rights to Congress. He also served as the fourth president of the United States.
Records and Information Management Month was introduced in 1995 by ARMA International (Association of Records Managers and Administrators) to recognize the crucial role of Records and Information Management (RIM) professionals. The month highlights the significant value they contribute to organizations and communities. As we celebrate its 31st anniversary, we honor April as RIM Month and the local professionals who dedicate themselves to the Records and Information Management field.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
In the 2025 Legislative Session, the State passed legislation (SB 954, adopted as 2025-182) which requires the governing body of each county or municipality to adopt an ordinance establishing procedures for the review and approval of certified recovery residences within its jurisdiction. The ordinance must include a process for requesting a reasonable accommodation from any local land use regulation that serves to prohibit the establishment of a certified recovery residence.”
Florida Statutes, Section 397.311, defines Recovery Residence as “a residential dwelling unit, the community housing component of a licensed day or night treatment facility with community housing, or other form of group housing, which is offered or advertised through any means, including oral, written, electronic, or printed means, by any person or entity as a residence that provides a peer-supported, alcohol-free, and drug-free living environment.”
A Certified Recovery Residence is further defined as “a recovery residence that holds a valid certificate of compliance and is actively managed by a certified recovery residence administrator (…who holds a valid certificate of compliance ... issued by a credentialing entity …)”
The Highlands County Land Development Regulations (“LDRs”) do not currently contain a directly comparable definition. The closest comparable definitions, which could be interpreted to include recovery residences, are as follows:
32A. Boarding home for sheltered care. A boarding home for the sheltered care of persons with special needs, which, in addition to providing food and shelter, may also provide some combination of personal care, social or counseling services, and transportation. See "assisted living facility; boardinghouse; community residences for the developmentally disabled; community shelters for victims of domestic violence."
55A. Community residences for the developmentally disabled. A residential facility, licensed by the state, providing food, shelter, and personal guidance, with supervision, to developmentally disabled or mentally ill persons who require assistance, temporarily or permanently, in order to live in the community and shall include group homes, halfway houses, intermediate care facilities, supervised apartment living arrangements, and hostels.
62A. Congregate living facility. Apartments and dwellings with communal dining facilities and services, such as housekeeping, organized social and recreational activities, transportation services, and other support services appropriate for the residents. (See community residential home #55B).
Any of the above defined uses would be permitted by right in the R-3, R-3 NC, B-1, B-2, B-3, and B-4 zoning districts. The existing LDRs do not provide a process for requesting a reasonable accommodation for relief from any land use regulation. After reviewing the State legislation and the County’s LDR provisions, the County Attorney has determined that an amendment to the County LDRs is warranted.
The purpose of this Statement of Legislative Intent is to receive input and direction from the Board for staff to pursue drafting amendments to the Land Development Regulations to establish a procedure for requesting a reasonable accommodation to the extent the County’s LDRs may serve to prohibit the establishment of a certified recovery residence.
Because this is a statutory requirement, and would be creating regulations that are more permissive, such amendments would not fall under the purview of SB 180, which prohibits the adoption of development regulations that are more restrictive or burdensome for the time period proscribed therein.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Consideration of Statement of Legislative Intent seeking direction from the Board to draft revisions to the Highlands County Land Development Regulations to establish procedures for Certified Recovery Residences.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description: The Board of County Commissioners approved the Ridge to River Conservation Planning Study in October 2024, utilizing the conservation trust fund. This two-year study conducted by the North Florida Land Trust will determine if the community is interested in a land conservation program. A Board workshop was held in March 2025 to rank the Board’s environmental priorities. This was followed by three (3) public workshops held in October 2025 to also rank and prioritize the community’s conservation values. In addition to the public workshops, an online survey was conducted and open to the citizens of Highlands County for three weeks. Based on results from the Board and the community, the attached Highlands County Land Conservation Program Green print was created. This suggested conservation manual recommends principles and procedures relative to what has been done in other counties to identify, assess, acquire, and steward lands for the Highlands County residents. A consensus from the Board to accept the Green print is needed before the next step of the process commences. If accepted, detailed polling will begin to determine the community’s desire for a conservation program, as well as their opinion on acceptable costs residents’ would pay to fund it. The result of this data is to be expected this spring and will be presented to the Board for review. At that time, a vote will be needed to proceed with placing the referendum language on the ballot for 2026 elections (November). Today is just an overview of the Green print with a required consensus to proceed with the polling.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Request acceptance of Ridge to River Conservation Planning Study Greenprint.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
Historically, the Highlands County Tax Collector collected the Tourist Development Tax (TDT) on behalf of the County. During that period, the Tax Collector’s Office was able to provide supplemental reporting, including breakdowns of TDT collections by zip code, as well as assistance with education and outreach to lodging operators regarding compliance with TDT requirements. This level of detail and local support enhanced the County’s understanding of where tourism activity was occurring and helped improve overall compliance.
In or around 2018, the Tax Collector’s Office transitioned to a software system that was not compatible with TDT administration, which necessitated moving TDT collection responsibilities to the Florida Department of Revenue. While the Department of Revenue provides statewide collection services, its reporting does not include detailed origin data such as geographic source (zip code) or accommodation type. As a result, the TDC has had limited insight into where TDT revenue is being generated within Highlands County.
The Highlands County Tax Collector has since implemented a new software system that is capable of supporting TDT collections. With this capability restored, the TDC proposes returning TDT collection responsibilities to the Tax Collector’s Office in order to:
Obtain more detailed and localized data regarding the source of TDT collections, including zip code and type of lodging; and
Allow the Tax Collector’s Office to provide education, outreach, and limited compliance assistance to ensure that all lodging operators required to collect and remit TDT in Highlands County are doing so.
Under this arrangement, the Tax Collector’s Office would receive a service fee equal to three percent (3%) of TDT collections, consistent with statutory allowances. The TDC believes that the enhanced data, improved local education efforts, and increased compliance opportunities will provide value that outweighs the associated administrative cost.
The TDC voted in favor of returning TDT collections to the local Tax Collector’s office at their October 30, 2025 Quarterly Board Meeting.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Statement of legislative intent authorizing the return of Tourist Development Tax collection duties from the Florida Department of Revenue to the Highlands County Tax Collector’s office.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
The Lake Istokpoga Management Committee (LIMC) was formed when the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC), formerly called the Florida Game and Freshwater Fish Commission, created an agreement with Highlands County to establish Lake Istokpoga as a Fish Management Area in 1997. The County terms of that agreement mandated that a committee (LIMC) be formed with the County responsible for managing all documents and records associated. In 2014, Highlands County adopted Resolution 14-15-47, setting the protocols for the composition, nomination, rotation, election, meeting mission and authority of the Lake Istokpoga Management Committee as part of the County’s obligations under the 1997 cooperative Agreement with the FWC.Since the agreement was signed, several new initiatives and management programs, such as the Lake Istokpoga Habitat Management Plan of 2020, have emerged that address the same objectives outlined in the 1997 Agreement. FWC has also developed more modern, comprehensive management protocols that are no longer dependent on the initial cooperative Agreement. These new programs incorporate advances in ecological research, technology, and sustainable management practices, ensuring the ongoing health and sustainability of Lake Istokpoga’s fisheries.
While the Agreement between Highlands County and FWC served its purpose in the late 90s, evolving circumstances such as the establishment of new initiatives, changes in management practices, and a greater role for local stakeholders have rendered the original Agreement unnecessary. The current landscape of fisheries management is now more capable of supporting Lake Istokpoga's needs without a formal partnership, making the Agreement redundant. Notwithstanding the termination of the Agreement, the County will remain active in its collection of the necessary data associated with Lake Istokpoga, to include assisting in habitat restoration, vegetation surveys, water quality, and will continue reporting the same to FWC.
The request to adopt Resolution No. 25-26-88, repealing Resolution No. 14-15-47, and dissolution of the LIMC, the County recognizes the advancements in stakeholder involvement and the evolution of the management plan. While the purpose of LIMC has diminished with other public meeting opportunities present, the County acknowledges FWC as the primary party in the management of the lake and will continue to be involved in collaborative efforts of Lake Istokpoga, as is accomplished on all other State waterbodies within the County. The County supports the public outreach and meetings established under FWC and will transition our involvement from a Committee chair of a State waterbody to an adequate voice on the habitat and management of Lake Istokpoga. This dissolution will alleviate ongoing responsibilities, tasks, and costs associated with quarterly meetings and record keeping while concurrently preserving the County’s desire to actively work with State agencies for the benefit of our residents.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title:
Request approval to
A) adopt Resolution No. 25-26-88, repealing Resolution No. 14-15-47 and dissolving the Lake Istokpoga Management Committee (LIMC) and
B) terminate the 1997 agreement with the Florida Game and Fresh Water Commission, now known as the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC).

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
In 1992, the State Legislature passed the Sadowski Affordable Housing Act. This affordable housing program is funded through documentary tax stamps on deeds recorded in Florida. The State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program provides services that develop and improve the economic condition of the community. Every three (3) years, Highlands County is required to submit a new three (3) year local housing assistance plan to the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. The Local Housing Assistance Plan (LHAP) governs the expenditures of the SHIP Program. The term of the LHAP is for three years. However, the plan can be amended.
The local housing assistance plans are intended to increase the availability of affordable residential units by combining local resources and cost-saving measures into a local housing partnership and using private and public funds to reduce the cost of housing.
According to Florida Statute, Chapter 420.9075, local housing assistance plans are to be created to make affordable residential units available to persons of very low income, low income, or moderate income and to persons who have special housing needs, including, but not limited to, homeless people, the elderly, migrant farm workers, and persons with disabilities.
We are requesting approval of Resolution # 25-26-075 repealing Resolution #21-22-145 for Amendment #2 of the 2022-2025 LHAP, including revised Exhibits including: Exhibit A- Administrative Budget; Exhibit B- Timeline for SHIP Expenditures; Exhibit C- Housing Delivery Goals Chart; Exhibit D- Certification to Floria Housing Finance Corporation; Exhibit E- Executed Resolution.
The 2022-2025 LHAP Plan Amendment #2 (Plan Amendment #1 approved by the Board of County Commissioners on November 1, 2022) as presented includes the addition and revision of strategies previously approved by the Highlands County Board of County Commissioners for the 2025-2028 LHAP (November 4, 2025).
SHIP funds must be expended three years from the time they were first received. As such, the funding received for Fiscal Year 2022-2023 (Project 21366 with an allocation of $987,773) was required to be expended by 06/30/2025. Funding received for Fiscal Year 2023-2024 (Project 22366 with an allocation of 1.2 mil) must be expended by 06/30/2026. Funding received for Fiscal Year 2024-2025 (Project 23366 with an allocation of $794,441) must be expended by 06/30/2027.
The 2022-2025 LHAP Amendment #2 reflects the community need for more affordable housing (May 2025 Housing Study conducted by Kimley-Horn), and assistance for special needs populations as defined in Florida Statute 420.0004 (13). The changing housing market now necessitates strategies which encourage homeownership, prevent property value decline, and build more resilient housing.
The attached matrix demonstrates the requested revisions including the introduction of sub-recipients and sponsors and added new strategies.
meeting: Regular Board of County Commissioners Meeting
title: Request approval of Resolution #25-26-075 of Amendment #2 of the 2022-2025 Local Housing Assistance Plan.

Highlands County is required to establish an Affordable Housing Advisory Committee (AHAC). The AHAC is responsible for reviewing and evaluating local plans, policies, procedures; land development regulations; the Goals, Policies and Objectives of the Comprehensive Plan; and other aspects of the County's housing activities that impact the production and provision of affordable housing.
The key role of the AHAC is to prepare the AHAC Incentive Strategy Report and evaluate its implementation annually. The Incentive Strategy Report identifies incentive strategies and recommendations for adoption by the local government. The recommendations are developed to remove regulatory barriers that limit the development or preservation of affordable housing or drive-up housing costs. The recommendations also suggest policies that encourage the production of affordable housing.
The Incentive Strategy Report summarizes the AHAC's findings and recommendations.

description:
The Affordable Housing Advisory Committee was created by Ordinance to review the established policies, procedures, ordinance, land development regulations and adopted comprehensive plan of the County, and to recommend specific initiatives to encourage or facilitate affordable housing while protecting the ability of the property to appreciate in value.
The Committee consists of at least 8, but not more than 11 members, and includes at least one local elected county official. Members must be representatives from the following categories:
(1) One citizen who is actively engaged in the banking or mortgage industry in connection with affordable housing. (VACANT)
(2) One citizen who is actively engaged as an advocate for low-income persons in connection with affordable housing.
(3) One citizen who is actively engaged in the residential home building industry in connection with affordable housing.
(4) One citizen who is actively engaged as a real estate professional in connection with affordable housing.
(5) One citizen who is a representative of those areas of labor actively engaged in home building in connection with affordable housing.
(6) One citizen who represents employers within the jurisdiction of Highlands County.
(7) One citizen who resides within the jurisdiction of Highlands County.
(8) One citizen who actively serves on the local planning agency pursuant to F.S. § 163.3174.
(9) One citizen who represents essential services personnel, as defined in the Highlands County Housing Assistance Program. (VACANT)
(10) One citizen who is actively engaged as a for-profit provider of affordable housing. (VACANT)

description:
On December 16, 2025, the list of proposed holidays to be observed in 2026, was presented to the Board for adoption. Upon further review, it was determined that the proposed New Year's Eve holiday on Thursday, December 31, 2026, was incorrectly reflected as one of the Board's "eleven (11) standard holidays" that the Board has observed for many years. While New Year's Eve was correctly identified as one of the holidays that the Tenth Judicial Circuit will be observing in 2026, the suggested motion provided to the Board did not accurately include it as an additional holiday. Staff will remove New Year's Eve 2026 from the list of holidays to be observed, and make any organizational adjustments necessary to staff-level deadlines that may be affected.
The corrected list of holidays for 2026, is noted as follows:
New Year's Day, Thursday, January 1, 2026 (previously approved by the Board on 09/05/24). Martin Luther King Day, Monday, January 19, 2026
Good Friday, Friday, April 3, 2026
Memorial Day, Monday, May 25, 2026
Independence Day, Friday, July 3, 2026
Labor Day, Monday, September 7, 2026
Veteran's Day (Observed), Wednesday, November 11, 2026
Thanksgiving Day, Thursday, November 26, 2026
Friday after Thanksgiving, Friday, November 27, 2026
Christmas Eve, Thursday, December 24, 2026
Christmas Day, Friday, December 25, 2026
New Year's Day Friday, January 1, 2027

description:
The Tourism Development Council’s (TDC) Public Relations services have been negotiated through an agreement with MuchPR for Fiscal Year 2025–2026 (October 1, 2025 – September 30, 2026). Under this agreement, MuchPR will continue to promote Highlands County as a travel destination through strategic media outreach, press trip coordination, and story development highlighting local events and attractions such as the Caladium Festival and Sebring Soda Festival.
MuchPR, led by Tanya Churchmuch, has represented Highlands County for several years and secured earned media coverage in outlets including USA Today, Southern Living, Travel + Leisure, and Afar. The firm’s longstanding familiarity with Highlands County's history, people, and visitor experiences, combined with its established relationships with regional, national, and international media, positions it to effectively promote the destination and generate earned media coverage.
At its August 7, 2025 meeting, the TDC voted in favor of entering into this agreement, allocating $39,600.00 of the TDC’s annual budget for the services rendered.

description:
Traditionally, the Board has adopted the same list of holidays observed by the Tenth Judicial Circuit, with minor modifications. Board minutes indicate that in 2012, the Board directed staff to survey the Constitutional Officers concerning the holidays they would be observing. Staff brought back the results of their survey, and from that the Board adopted a schedule of eleven (11) standard holidays they would observe each year and further directed that the list of standard holidays be reflected in the Board’s Personnel Manual. category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
description:
At its October 30, 2025 meeting, the Tourist Development Council (TDC) approved the attached policies for its grant funding programs. The updated policy framework includes revisions to existing grant categories and introduces two new programs designed to further the County’s strategic tourism development goals.
The revised High Impact Signature Event Grant Policy updates eligibility and reporting requirements, adds a defined grant agreement process, expands insurance and compliance standards, and introduces a scoring-based funding structure that ties a portion of reimbursement to marketing performance. The revisions also clarify eligible uses of funds, streamline administrative procedures, and align the program with current County practices and Visit Sebring branding standards.
Upon Board approval, the updated policies will take effect immediately and apply to all new grant applications considered at the January 2026 TDC meeting and thereafter.

At its October 30, 2025 meeting, the Tourist Development Council (TDC) voted to recommend Board approval of a new Tourism Marketing Assistance Program (TMAP) policy as part of the overall update to the TDC’s grant funding framework.
The TMAP program is designed to assist Highlands County tourism-related businesses—such as attractions, outfitters, and cultural or heritage sites—in developing out-of-county marketing initiatives and tourism-focused promotional efforts that attract visitors and encourage extended stays during non-peak months (April–December). The reimbursable program supports eligible marketing and advertising expenses including digital and e-marketing campaigns, website enhancements, and other initiatives that strengthen the Visit Sebring brand and drive visitation to Highlands County. This new program aligns with the County’s strategic tourism development goals by expanding opportunities for smaller tourism partners to reach broader visitor markets and by promoting balanced, year-round tourism growth.
Upon Board approval, the updated policies will take effect immediately and apply to all new grant applications considered at the January 2026 TDC meeting and thereafter.

category: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
